title: Life Experiences: Present Perfect for Experience
canDo: Can describe past experiences and personal history, and explain them with simple reasons.
goal: Talk about life experiences using have or has with the past participle, and discover when to use it.

warmup.prompt: Ask an open question: Have you ever done something unusual? Give a 15-second example: I have climbed a mountain. It was tiring but amazing.
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student speak for 1 to 2 minutes without interruption. Note two target structures for the wrap-up.

theory.structure: Subject + have / has + past participle (ever, never, already, yet)
examples: I have visited Spain twice.
Have you ever tried sushi?
She has never flown on a plane.
theory.method: Show the three sentences in context and ask guiding questions: When did the action happen? Do we know the exact time? Then ask the student to state the rule in their own words.
theory.checkQuestion: Do we know the exact time when the action happened, or does it matter only that it happened in life?

comprehension.source: Listen to a short podcast extract or read this text twice at normal speed: My grandfather has worked as a fisherman for forty years. He has seen many storms, but he says he has never stopped loving the sea. Last year he finally retired, and he has already started teaching his grandchildren to sail.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: How long has the grandfather worked as a fisherman? (forty years). What has he already started doing? (teaching grandchildren to sail).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: What is the main idea of the text? Ask the student to infer the grandfather's attitude to the sea and point to the phrase that shows it.

conversation.task: Life experience discussion: the student tells the tutor about three experiences they have had (travel, food, work, hobbies). The tutor listens without interrupting and asks one follow-up question: What was the best part?
conversation.mandate: Do not interrupt mid-sentence. Let the student speak for at least 60 to 65 percent of the class and note mistakes silently for the wrap-up.

mistakes: I have visit Spain twice.
Have you ever eat sushi?

title: Present Perfect or Past Simple: Choosing the Right Tense
canDo: Can distinguish between finished past events and past experiences that connect to the present.
goal: Choose between present perfect and past simple by discovering the time-reference rule.

warmup.prompt: Ask: What is one thing you have lost recently? Give a 15-second example: I have lost my keys, so I am late. Last week I lost my wallet.
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student speak freely for 1 to 2 minutes. Record two tense choices for later discussion.

theory.structure: Present perfect (have / has + past participle) for result now; past simple (verb + ed or irregular) for a finished time
examples: I have lost my keys. (I cannot open the door now.)
I lost my keys yesterday. (The event is finished.)
She has finished the report. She finished it at noon.
theory.method: Show the two example pairs side by side. Ask guiding questions: Is there a finished time word? Does the event affect now? Let the student match each sentence to the rule.
theory.checkQuestion: Which sentence has a finished time word, and which one connects to the present?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice at normal speed: Ana has moved to a new flat. She moved there last month. Since then she has met many neighbours, and she has finally found a good bakery nearby.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: When did Ana move? (last month). What has she met? (many neighbours). What has she found? (a good bakery).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: How does Ana feel about her new home? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the main idea, such as finally found a good bakery.

conversation.task: Story and result: the student tells the tutor about a recent event (a lost item, a finished project, a visit) using both tenses. The tutor asks: What happened next? Has it changed anything now?
conversation.mandate: Do not interrupt mid-sentence. Let the student choose the tense first, and keep the wrap-up for corrections.

mistakes: I have lost my keys yesterday.
She has finished it at noon.

title: If It Rains: First Conditional
canDo: Can talk about likely future situations and their consequences in familiar contexts.
goal: Describe a likely future situation and its result using if with the present simple and will.

warmup.prompt: Ask: What will you do if it rains tomorrow? Give a 15-second example: If it rains, I will stay home and read.
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student speak freely for 1 to 2 minutes. Note any if-clause patterns for the wrap-up.

theory.structure: If + present simple, will + base verb (the condition is likely)
examples: If you study tonight, you will pass the test.
If it is sunny, we will go to the beach.
She will call you if she has time.
theory.method: Show two example sentences with the if-clause first and then with the main clause first. Ask guiding questions: What is the condition? What is the result? Which verb form is used after if?
theory.checkQuestion: After if, do we use will or the present simple?

comprehension.source: Listen to a short weather forecast or read this text twice: If the wind gets stronger tomorrow, the ferries will stop running. If that happens, many people will take the train instead.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What will stop if the wind gets stronger? (the ferries). What will many people take? (the train).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the speaker certain about the ferries stopping, or only expecting it? Ask the student to point to the word that shows this, such as if.

conversation.task: Plans and consequences: the student describes three plans for next weekend, each with an if-condition and a result. The tutor asks one follow-up question: What will you do if the plan changes?
conversation.mandate: Do not interrupt mid-sentence. Let the student speak for at least 60 to 65 percent of the class and encourage longer answers.

mistakes: If it will rain, I will stay home.
If you will study, you pass.

title: Advice and Rules: Should, Must, and Have To
canDo: Can give advice, express obligations, and explain rules in familiar situations using modal verbs.
goal: Give advice and talk about obligations using should, must, and have to.

warmup.prompt: Ask: What is one rule at your workplace or school? Give a 15-second example: You have to wear a badge at work.
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student speak freely for 1 to 2 minutes. Note modal verbs for the wrap-up.

theory.structure: Subject + should (advice) / must (strong obligation) / have to (external rule) + base verb
examples: You should drink more water.
You must lock the door when you leave.
We have to wear uniforms at this school.
theory.method: Show the three examples. Ask guiding questions: Who makes the rule? Is it a suggestion or a requirement? Then ask the student to decide which modal fits each situation.
theory.checkQuestion: If a rule comes from the company, do we use must or have to?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice: New employees should read the safety guide before they start. They have to wear helmets on the factory floor, and they must never leave the machines running when no one is there.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What should new employees read? (the safety guide). What do they have to wear? (helmets). What must they never do? (leave the machines running).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the tone of the text friendly or strict? Ask the student to point to the word that shows the level of obligation, such as must.

conversation.task: Advice column: the student reads a short problem card (a friend is always late; a neighbour plays loud music) and gives advice to the tutor using should, must, or have to. The tutor responds with one question.
conversation.mandate: Do not interrupt mid-sentence. Let the student finish the advice before responding, and keep the wrap-up for modal corrections.

mistakes: You should to drink more water.
You must to wear a helmet.

title: Past Habits: Used To
canDo: Can describe past habits and states that are no longer true, using everyday examples.
goal: Talk about past habits and changes using used to and did not use to.

warmup.prompt: Ask: How has your life changed in the last five years? Give a 15-second example: I used to live in a small town. Now I live in the city.
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student speak freely for 1 to 2 minutes and note habit verbs for later.

theory.structure: Subject + used to + base verb (past habit or state, no longer true); did not use to for negatives
examples: I used to play football every weekend.
She used to be very shy.
We did not use to eat meat.
theory.method: Show the examples with the present situation beside each. Ask guiding questions: Is this true now? Is it a habit that has stopped? Let the student contrast a past habit with a present habit.
theory.checkQuestion: Does used to describe something that is still true now?

comprehension.source: Listen to a short podcast extract or read this text twice: When I was young, we used to walk to school every day. We did not use to have phones, so we played outside. Now my children take the bus, and they spend more time on screens.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: How did the speaker go to school? (walked). What did they not have? (phones). What do the children do now? (take the bus, use screens).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Does the speaker see the change as good or bad? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the attitude, such as spend more time on screens.

conversation.task: Then and now: the student describes one habit they had as a child and one they have now. The tutor asks: What made you change?
conversation.mandate: Do not interrupt mid-sentence. Let the student speak for 60 to 65 percent of the class and encourage a longer answer for the reason.

mistakes: I use to play football.
I didn't used to like coffee.

title: Predictions and Plans: Will or Going To
canDo: Can make predictions and talk about plans and intentions in familiar contexts, explaining the reasons.
goal: Use will for predictions and going to for plans, and explain the difference in context.

warmup.prompt: Ask: What do you think the world will be like in twenty years? Give a 15-second example: I think cars will drive themselves.
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student speak freely for 1 to 2 minutes and note the forms they use.

theory.structure: Will + base verb (prediction or instant decision); am / is / are going to + base verb (plan or evidence now)
examples: I think it will rain later.
Look at those clouds. It is going to rain.
I will call you back in a minute.
theory.method: Show the three examples. Ask guiding questions: Is there evidence now? Was the decision made before speaking? Let the student sort each example into prediction, plan, or instant decision.
theory.checkQuestion: In Look at those clouds, is the prediction based on evidence now or a decision made in the moment?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice: The company is going to open a new office next year because sales have grown. Many experts think the city will become a major business centre in the next decade.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What is the company going to open? (a new office). Why? (sales have grown). What do experts think will happen? (the city will become a major business centre).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the writer certain about the business centre prediction? Ask the student to find the word that shows the level of certainty, such as think.

conversation.task: Prediction debate: the student makes two predictions about technology or the environment and gives a reason for each using because. The tutor offers one counter-prediction.
conversation.mandate: Do not interrupt mid-sentence. Let the student finish both predictions before responding, and keep corrections for the wrap-up.

mistakes: I think it going to rain.
Look at the clouds. It will rain.

title: Passive Voice: How Things Are Made
canDo: Can describe processes, products, and events where the action is more important than who does it.
goal: Describe how something is made or was built using the passive voice in simple tenses.

warmup.prompt: Show a photo of a bridge. Ask: Who do you think built this bridge, and when?
warmup.tutorAction: Give a 15-second example: This bridge was built in 1950. Let the student speak freely and note the verb forms.

theory.structure: Object + am / is / are (present) or was / were (past) + past participle (+ by + agent if needed)
examples: Bread is made from flour and water.
The factory was built in 1990.
The letters were sent yesterday by post.
theory.method: Show the passive pattern on screen beside an active sentence. Ask guiding questions: Who does the action? Is the action or the doer more important? Let the student change one active sentence into the passive.
theory.checkQuestion: In The factory was built, is the focus on the builders or on the factory?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice: Coffee is grown in many tropical countries. The beans are picked by hand, then they are dried and roasted. Finally, the coffee is packed and sent to shops around the world.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: Where is coffee grown? (tropical countries). How are the beans picked? (by hand). What happens to the coffee at the end? (it is packed and sent to shops).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Does the writer focus on the people who grow the coffee or on the process? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the focus, such as are picked by hand.

conversation.task: Process explanation: the student explains how a familiar product or meal is made using at least three passive sentences. The tutor asks one question: Who usually does this step?
conversation.mandate: Do not interrupt mid-sentence. Let the student explain the whole process first, then note passive errors for the wrap-up.

mistakes: Bread is make from flour.
The factory was build in 1990.

title: Describing People and Things: Relative Clauses
canDo: Can describe people, places, and things in more detail by joining ideas into one sentence.
goal: Describe people and objects using who, which, and that in relative clauses.

warmup.prompt: Show a photo of a busy market. Ask: What is one thing you can see here that you like?
warmup.tutorAction: Give a 15-second example: I like the stall that sells fresh fruit. Let the student describe one or two details.

theory.structure: Noun + who (people) / which or that (things) + verb or subject, to add information
examples: The woman who lives next door is a doctor.
This is the book which I bought yesterday.
The café that opened last week is very busy.
theory.method: Show the three examples. Ask guiding questions: Is the noun a person or a thing? Which word joins the two ideas? Let the student join two short sentences into one with who or which.
theory.checkQuestion: Do we use who or which for a person?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice: My teacher, who lives near the river, always brings homemade bread. The bakery that she uses is famous for its sourdough, which takes three days to make.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: Who brings homemade bread? (the teacher). Where does she live? (near the river). How long does the sourdough take? (three days).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Does the speaker respect or dislike the teacher? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the attitude, such as always brings homemade bread.

conversation.task: Describe and guess: the student describes a person or object they know, using at least two relative clauses. The tutor tries to guess who or what it is, then asks: Can you tell me more about the place?
conversation.mandate: Do not interrupt mid-sentence. Let the student finish each description before guessing, and note relative-pronoun errors for the wrap-up.

mistakes: The woman which lives next door.
The book who I bought is good.

title: Reporting What People Said: Reported Speech
canDo: Can report what someone said or wrote in a simple, accurate way.
goal: Report statements and questions from the past using said that and asked with a tense change.

warmup.prompt: Ask: What did your manager or teacher say to you last week? Give a 15-second example: My teacher said that the test would be on Monday.
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student speak freely for 1 to 2 minutes and note any reported speech for later.

theory.structure: Subject + said / told + (that) + statement with the tense moved back one step (is becomes was; will becomes would)
examples: She said, I am tired. She said that she was tired.
He said, I will call you. He said he would call me.
They asked, Where do you live? They asked where I lived.
theory.method: Show direct speech on the left and reported speech on the right. Ask guiding questions: What changed in the tense? What changed in the pronoun? Let the student report one thing a friend said.
theory.checkQuestion: When we report a question, do we keep the question word order or change it?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice: Yesterday my manager told us that the meeting had moved to Friday. She also said that the new software would arrive next week and asked us to read the manual.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: When is the meeting now? (Friday). When will the software arrive? (next week). What did the manager ask them to do? (read the manual).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the manager's tone urgent or relaxed? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the tone, such as asked us to read.

conversation.task: Relay game: the tutor says a short statement or question. The student reports it to a third person (for example, to a colleague). Then the student reports one thing the tutor said earlier in the lesson.
conversation.mandate: Do not interrupt mid-sentence. Let the student finish the report before correcting, and keep tense errors for the wrap-up.

mistakes: She said that she is tired.
He asked me where do I live.

title: Contrast and Concession: However, Although, and Despite
canDo: Can connect ideas that contrast or contradict each other using linking words, in familiar topics.
goal: Link contrasting ideas with although, however, and despite, and explain the contrast clearly.

warmup.prompt: Ask: Is there something you enjoy even though it is difficult? Give a 15-second example: I enjoy running, although it is hard in the heat.
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student speak freely for 1 to 2 minutes and note the linking words they use.

theory.structure: Although + clause (sentence), / Despite + noun or -ing, / The sentence. However, + new idea.
examples: Although it was cold, we went swimming.
Despite the rain, the match continued.
The food was cheap. However, it was not very tasty.
theory.method: Show the three patterns with the contrast in each sentence highlighted. Ask guiding questions: What is the expected result? What is the surprising result? Let the student join two ideas with although.
theory.checkQuestion: After despite, do we use a full clause or a noun or -ing form?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice: Although the city has many parks, most people prefer to stay indoors in winter. However, the council is building new cycle paths, despite the budget cuts.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What do most people prefer in winter? (to stay indoors). What is the council building? (new cycle paths). What is the problem with the budget? (budget cuts).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the writer positive or negative about the council's plan? Ask the student to point to the linking word that shows the contrast, such as however.

conversation.task: Balanced argument: the student gives two sides of a topic (for example, working from home) using although and however. The tutor responds with one counter-point and asks: What is your final opinion?
conversation.mandate: Do not interrupt mid-sentence. Let the student build the full contrast before responding, and keep linking-word errors for the wrap-up.

mistakes: Although it was cold, but we went swimming.
Despite it rained, we went out.
